summary: A response to RFC 606 about providing Host names on-line, one of several related notes with RFCs 623, 625 and 627. It was replaced by RFC 810.

plainLanguage.summary: Another note about sharing a list of computer names. A later paper replaced it.

questions: what was the nics host list
how did early networks find host addresses
subtitle: Keeping computers findable with an online list of host names and addresses

tldr.problem: Early networks had no central way to find host addresses. Engineers had to manually coordinate or exchange lists of computer names and their numeric addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC proposes to maintain a single online ASCII file containing official host names, network addresses, and status attributes, generated from a central database and available via FTP.
tldr.outcome: This became a foundational idea for host name directories, though the specific syntax was soon superseded by RFC 810 and later the DNS system.

today: RFC 608 is marked Unknown status. It was replaced by RFC 810, which introduced an improved format. The concept evolved into the HOSTS.TXT file and eventually the DNS system.

sections.title: The Need for a Central Host List
sections.content:
RFC 608 responds to an earlier proposal in RFC 606 by Peter Deutsch. The NIC (Network Information Center) at SRI-ARC agrees that the growing ARPANET needs a single, machine-readable file listing all known hosts: their official names, their network addresses, and key attributes like whether each host is a server, user machine, or terminal interface processor (TIP).

Rather than having each site maintain its own partial list and try to keep them in sync, one authoritative source would be generated regularly from a central database and made available to all.
sections.plainLanguage: Growing networks needed a master list of all the computers and their addresses. This document says the NIC should keep that list, update it regularly, and let everyone download it.

sections.title: File Format and Entry Structure
sections.content:
Each entry in the ASCII file contains two parts: a basic entry and optional attributes. The basic entry is a host name and its decimal network address, separated by a comma. Attribute entries follow, with names and values on separate lines.

A host name is up to 48 characters: letters, digits, and hyphens only, starting with a letter and never ending with a hyphen. For hosts not on the ARPANET, the official network name can prefix the host name in parentheses (up to 24 characters, with the same character restrictions). Initially, the only attribute is STATUS, which takes one of four values: SERVER, USER, TIP, or UNKNOWN. Future attributes (nicknames, FTP byte sizes, terminal echo modes) are planned but not yet included in the file.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line lists a computer's name and address. Names follow simple rules: letters, numbers, and hyphens, nothing else. Each computer is marked as a SERVER, USER machine, or TIP. More details could be added later.

sections.title: Availability and Updates
sections.content:
The NIC will generate the file on a schedule (initially weekly or as needed) and store it at host OFFICE-1 (host address 43 decimal) under the pathname <NETINFO>HOSTS.TXT. The file is accessible via FTP with guest login (username GUEST, password ARPA, account 1). The file is sorted alphabetically by host name.

The RFC invites suggestions for additional attributes and welcomes comments from the community.
sections.plainLanguage: The file sits on one computer that everyone can reach using FTP. It gets updated regularly and is organized in alphabetical order so you can search it easily.

references.text: Deutsch, P., "Specification of Internetwork Naming Units", RFC 606, January 1974.
